summary.text: 能 is interpreted as a picture of a bear-like animal. It is also attested with the meanings “be able” and “ability,” but the evidence does not show how those uses connect to the bear sense.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph is interpreted as depicting a bear-like animal. The proposed Shang examples are disputed; securely identified examples are placed in Western Zhou bronze by one paleographic account. The Han dictionary instead analyzes the graph as 肉 plus 㠯, with 㠯 as a sound element, but that shape may reflect the altered bear head.

components.text: The graph is treated as one whole picture of a bear-like animal, with a head, body, limbs and short tail. The identification of damaged Shang forms as this character is disputed; the modern-looking parts are not separate components in this analysis.

history.text: One account identifies damaged Shang oracle-bone forms as 能 and describes changes toward Western Zhou bronze: the head becomes 㠯-like, the body is rendered as 月 (肉), and the feet are placed side by side. Another account rejects the Shang identification and places securely identifiable examples in Western Zhou bronze. The proposed Shang forms are too damaged to establish their use.

The Han dictionary defines 能 as a kind of bear and analyzes it as 肉 plus 㠯. It links the animal’s firmness and strength with 賢能 and 能傑; this is the dictionary’s explanation, not a demonstrated history connecting the bear and ability meanings.

uncertainties.text: Whether the damaged Shang forms are 能 remains disputed, and no precise first date for the Western Zhou examples is established. The evidence does not show whether “be able” developed from the bear word or whether the graph was reused for that word because of similar sounds.
The Han dictionary calls 㠯 a sound element, while graphic analysis allows that it represents the transformed bear head. No independent phonetic role or component sound comparison is established.

senses.text: The Han dictionary defines 能 as a kind of bear, and historical pronunciation records distinguish bear readings. The proposed Shang examples do not securely date this use because their identification and use are disputed.
A reported Western Zhou bronze use has 能 as a verb meaning “be able to.” This is the earliest ability use identified here; it does not establish the character’s original meaning.
Historical reports cite ability-related noun uses in Warring States-era texts. Modern definitions include “ability,” but do not establish a further dated stage.

limitations.text: The bear and ability uses are separately attested, but their semantic relationship or a sound-based borrowing between them is not established. The evidence gives no independently known spoken name for the depicted bear to demonstrate a sound match.

overview.text: 能 is traditionally interpreted as a picture of a bear-like animal, though the proposed Shang forms are disputed. It is also used for “be able” and “ability”; how these meanings connect to the bear sense is unclear.

items.period: Seal-script style associated with the Shuowen tradition; the vector file was uploaded in 2011 and is not an ancient artifact image.
items.caption: A later seal-script form of 能 associated with the Shuowen tradition. It offers a comparison with the disputed Shang readings but does not resolve them.
items.alt: Black seal-script strokes forming 能 on a plain white background.
items.selection_reason: This identifiable seal-script form provides a useful later written comparison. Its shape cannot verify the proposed bear interpretation of damaged Shang forms.
